author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: Thought and imagination. More on artificial intelligence
content: The issue of artificial intelligence, which is debated today not always with natural intelligence, has had a precursor in the history of Western philosophy — as we have already had occasion to demonstrate here —: the single, separate intellect of Latin Averroism. The analogy is so close — a single, separate intellect that thinks independently of individual human beings — that it may even coincide in the acronym used to express it: Artificial Intelligence – Agent Intellect (as the Averroists called the separate intellect). For medieval philosophers, who were more cautious in this regard than our contemporaries, the crucial problem was that of the manner in which the single, separate intellect unites (copulatur) with individual human beings, so that thought may be acquired (adeptus) by the individual and it may be said “hic homo intelligit“—”this man thinks”. The means by which this union is achieved was, for Averroes, the imagination, of which our contemporaries, by contrast, seem to be utterly deprived. In artificial intelligence, in fact, “hic homo non intellegit“—the individual renounces thinking and delegates the most precious of his faculties to a machine, which is supposed to think in his stead and better than he does. author: Julius Gavroche
title: Kojin Karatani: The Spectres of Sovereignty
content:
On Kojin Karatani’s 85th birthday, publisher Maikel da Silveira reflects on his writings on and the current US imperial project.

Maikel da Silveira, Verso Books Blog, 06/08/2026

The philosopher and literary critic Kojin Karatani turns 85 today. His latest book, The End of Modern Literature: On Permanent Revolution, publishes later this month. Meanwhile, his most ambitious work, The Structure of World History: From Modes of Production to Modes of Exchange – which I had the privilege of editing for Editora Machado – has been translated into Portuguese and should reach Brazilian readers in the coming months.

Both of Karatani’d books are arriving at an opportune moment. Recent actions by Donald Trump’s United States — such as the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro, the attacks on Iran, the tariff wars launched against several countries and, above all, the designation of criminal organizations from various countries as terrorist groups, as well as the application of the same label to left-wing organizations operating within the United States — have created a dangerous precedent for justifying US military interventions in sovereign states. We have seen this film before, in the Bush era and in the days of the War on Terror. But everything suggests that this new wave of interventionism will strike with far greater force and violence.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Martin Sostre: Follow the Principles that Won My Freedom
content:
The following speech, “Follow the Principles that Won My Freedom,” was delivered by Sostre in 1976 shortly after his release from prison and offers a message of revolutionary optimism about how collective action can succeed—as it did for him—in freeing political prisoners and building a new egalitarian society. It is a message that feels as urgent today as it did then… “Follow the Same Principles that Won My Freedom” by Martin Sostre is excerpted from I Cannot Submit to Injustices: Collected Works of Martin Sostre, edited by Garrett Felber and published by AK Press, reproduced with permission of Felber and AK Press.

It is a great pleasure to be here after being in prison for nine years. I was the victim of a frame-up because I fought for human rights and because I had the only bookstore in Buffalo, New York, that was disseminating socialist and political literature—literature dealing with the struggle for Black liberation here in this country, the struggle for Puerto Rican independence, literature against the war in Vietnam, and all progressive literature. That bookstore in Buffalo became a center for persons of conscience, for youths who were seeking guidance, for college students.

Naturally, the power structure did not like this, and as a result I was framed. And this is what happened in all of the Black ghettos, especially during the 1960s, and is still happening now.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: When  the house is on fire
content:
With fires literally raging across the world, we return to a 2020 essay by Giorgio Agamben.

Other languages: Italiano, Español, Français, Nederlands, Português, Russian, Deutsch, Greek, Magyar, Türkçe

“Nothing I’m doing makes any sense if the house is on fire.” Yet even when the house is on fire it is necessary to continue as before, to do everything with care and precision, perhaps even more so than before—even if no one notices. Perhaps life itself will disappear from the face of the earth, perhaps no memory whatsoever will remain of what has been done, for better or for worse. But you continue as before, it is too late to change, there is no time anymore.

“What’s happening around you / is no longer your business”. Like the geography of a country that you must leave behind forever. Yet how does it still affect you? Precisely now that it is no longer your business, now that everything seems over, everything and every place now appears in its truest guise, somehow they all touch you even more intimately—just as they are: splendor and poverty.

Philosophy, a dead language. “The language of poets is always a dead language…it is a strange thing to admit: a dead language that one uses to provide greater life to thought.” Perhaps not a dead language, but a dialect. author: Julius Gavroche
title: Reflections on a decade of UK Black Lives Matter
content:
From Freedom News (09/08/2026)

This racist violence we experience is an active race?making project serving the interests of capital

Black Lives Matter UK was founded by activists who had worked together on previous deaths in police custody, both in the US and Britain.

In the US, it had started as a love letter to Black people in the aftermath of George Zimmerman’s acquittal – who killed 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in 2012 for the crime of carrying Skittles while Black in a gated community.

In Britain our martyr was Mark Duggan, killed by the Met in 2011. We not only remember the anti-Black propaganda about his criminality, how even some radical leftists argued he needed to die, how the army needed to be brought in to control rioters. We remember the public disregard of his and Black life in general. We live with the reality of State harassment and violence in terms of stop and search, legal sexual assault in terms of strip searches. State racist violence is not only structural, it structures the British economy and State legitimacy.

Today, which is worse than in 2011, almost one in two Black children do not get three meals a day. Ethnically Black African children do better than white British children in GCSEs, but are less likely to get a paid job. All of this motivates us because it is our lived reality.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Italy’s war on occupied social centres
content:
In early June, we shared news about and a documentary film dedicated to “Spin Time”, an occupied social centre in the heart of Rome.

On the 29th of July, a small fire in the social centre’s building provided the occasion to evict the some 400 residents, including children, elderly and disabled people on to the street.

At this moment, it would seem that “Spin Time” has come to an end. Their struggle and ours however continues.

Angela Giuffrida, “Hundreds camp in Rome heatwave as Meloni government cracks down on squats”, The Guardian, 05/08/2026.

Angela Giuffrida, “Scramble to house hundreds camping in Rome heatwave after squat eviction”, The Guardian, 07/06/2026

Over the years, we have published numerous articles on the struggle for and significance of occupied social centres. Click here to review.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Franco “Bifo” Berardi: An apocalyptic left-wing culture must emerge
content:
We should have learnt long ago to think with two minds: the mind of the inevitable and that of the unpredictable. It is from this dual perspective that we should consider the spring of 2027, when the countries of Mediterranean Europe – Italy, Spain, France and Greece – will go to the polls.







We cannot be sure of anything when we consider the future course of the storm currently raging – not even that we will still be here in the spring of ’27, nor that the minimum conditions of civilisation required to hold political elections will still exist at that time. Russian and Ukrainian nationalism, Zionist Nazism and the Trumpist warmongering mafia are clenching the continent’s fate in a fist, whilst from within a black wave is rising and racists are preparing to deliver the coup de grâce in Germany and the United Kingdom.




But let us suppose that in a year’s time we are still here: in that case, in the Mediterranean region we must expect the possible triumph of a sinister form of idiocy, unless some unforeseen political innovation emerges – something of which the existing left is, evidently, incapable.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The origins of Black anarchism in Brazil
content:
From 

Freedom News

 (

23/07/2028

)







A brief historical overview of Black anarchist militance in the early Brazilian labour movement (1906-1930)




Carlos Junior




Although only a few pages have been dedicated to Black libertarian militants in Brazil, they were at the forefront of important events and achievements in the Brazilian labour movement.







The chronology would undoubtedly begin with the teacher, philosopher, and journalist Antônio Pedro de Figueiredo (1814–1859). Figueiredo founded the magazine 

O Progresso

 (1846–1848) which featured contributions from other writers who, like Figueiredo, were influenced by French “utopian” socialism.




In Recife during the 1840s, there was a small colony of French migrants, including the socialist engineer Louis Vauthier, who brought several books by socialist authors such as Saint-Simon, Owen, and Fourier, as well as the already self-proclaimed anarchist Proudhon. In 1849, Figueiredo condemned slavery and large landownership in Pernambuco based on Proudhon’s maxim: “destroy despotism embodied in large landed property.” Because of his socialist ideas, Figueiredo suffered constant racist insults from his opponents.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: A new hunting season has been declared (pt. 2), or the normalisation of fascism
content:
On the 16th of July, at the invitation of Marco Rubio and the US State Department, representatives of over 60 countries 

gathered

 to hear Rubio 

annonce

 that “the counterterrorism architecture of the free world, built over a generation against jihadist mass murder, should be rebuilt and aimed at the domestic left”, wherever it might show itself, for “the left”, in its many incarnations, is the implacable enemy of the “West” and its civilization.










This is a distinctive and unique evil.  It has always been driven by a hatred above all else, a hatred for civilization itself.  It is a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good.  It is perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.  This is what radical leftism is.  It may wear various different slogans and ideologies across place and time.  They can call themselves anti-capitalist or anti-imperialist or communist or anarchist or Marxist.  But the fundamental character is always the same.  It’s always the same. 




It is a poisonous resentment cloaked in the language of equality and justice and liberation, an overwhelming need to tear down what greater men have built, to wreck what is beautiful and what is right

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The 90th anniversary of the spanish revolution, today
content:
Manel Aisa Pàmpols, 

Redes Libertarias

, 20/07/2026




Trying to understand the anarchist movement in Barcelona, Catalonia, and the surrounding area in the early 20th century is by no means easy, but ultimately it is a phenomenon that is by no means new – it is a class struggle in the truest sense, which emerged, as in so many other parts of Europe and the Americas, with the development of the Industrial Revolution, when the bourgeoisie required a large workforce in the cities or in the industrial regions, and steam-powered machinery began to drive mass production; and so, faced with the need for a large workforce, the great migrations of the modern world began.







Initially, workers were offered appalling working and living conditions, and the bourgeoisie and capital paid scant heed to the needs that arose upon their arrival in the major cities.




All this took place against the backdrop of the First World War, during which Catalonia became the breadbasket of belligerent Europe.




This led to the amassing of great fortunes, following in the footsteps of the “Indianos” (returnees from the Americas), many of whom had already made their fortunes through the slave trade in the Americas during the 18th and 19th centuries.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Giorgio Agamben: The first friend and the first enemy
content:
Jacopo Pontormo, 

Portrait of two friends

, c. 1522







As a scientist friend of mine, who likes to reflect on such matters, writes to me, the fundamental event in the history of living beings was the emergence of a microorganism capable of feeling pain. This thesis must, of course, be clarified by placing “pleasure” before — or adding it to — “pain”. If we rate this fundamental capacity of living beings to what Aristotle writes about the perception of the sensation of existence (“to perceive that one lives is a thing pleasant in itself, life being a thing naturally good, and the perceiving of the presence in ourselves of things naturally good being pleasant”), we can then say that the primordial form of the capacity to feel pleasure or pain relates to the very fact of existing, to the sensation of being alive. The sensation of the sweetness of living is, in fact, matched by its symmetrically opposite counterpart, in which, for some reason—or even for no apparent reason at all—feeling that one is alive proves painful.







The quote from Aristotle that we have cited forms part of the treatise on friendship contained in Books VIII and IX of the 

Nicomachean Ethics

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Tomás Ibáñez: Anarchisms at the crossroads
content:
Redes Libertarias

 (

06/06/2026

)







Tomás Ibáñez’s essay, “Anarchism at the crossroads”, is an intervention in a debate in the Spanish anarchist milieu, but the controversy is neither uniquely Spanish nor novel.




What kind of organisation does anarchist politics call for? Must it have strategic or tactical goals, or both? How is it to be structured “internally”? What relationships should it have, if any, with other political organisations that share common ambitions, with people who have no organisational affiliation? Should the organisation in some way prefigure the “goals” of anarchism? Should such an organisation be bound to a particular “vision” of anarchism, should it heed to a binding ideology? Is a 

single

 anarchist organisation even desirable?




The questions, explicit and tacit, raised in the debate Ibáñez addresses are at the very heart of anarchism (and we could add, of the “socialist” tradition more broadly), and while he may not close it – he does not pretend to -, his intervention is important, perhaps even in ways that he has not expressed.




On this matter, we make our own the words of Herman Melville.
